evidence: The survivor uses "order vertices by decreasing degree (DSATUR-like heuristic)" and a three-color array; the defeated solutions likewise treat the constraint as graph coloring.
affordance_in_statement: The router computes the checksum as $(7 \times c_u + 13 \times c_v) \bmod 20$. A routing collision occurs if this checksum evaluates to exactly 0.
removal_suggestion: Make the collision relation genuinely non-equality-based and direction-dependent, rather than having zero checksum occur exactly when the two shard IDs are equal. For example, retain the stated checksum rule but additionally define (or encode in the checksum) the ordered pair (c_u,c_v)=(2,1) as a collision. This does not invalidate Example 1's assignment and leaves Example 2 impossible, while preventing a reduction to plain 3-coloring.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Recognizes or effectively treats every edge as requiring different colors, then applies DSATUR-like backtracking for 3-coloring.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: The checksum is zero for exactly (c_u,c_v)=(1,1),(2,2),(3,3), so every listed pair is simply a graph edge requiring unequal colors.

common_affordance: The checksum-zero condition is exactly equality of the two shard IDs, reducing the task to ordinary graph 3-coloring.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: Uses straightforward vertex-order backtracking over three colors, which can take exponential time on hard 3-coloring instances with n=40.
Also uses exhaustive/backtracking-style coloring after precomputing forbidden shard pairs, leading to exponential search and TLE.

recommended_edit: Change the mutable collision semantics so that, in addition to equal shard IDs, at least one direction-specific unequal shard pair is forbidden—for example, declare (c_u,c_v)=(2,1) a collision as well. This preserves the supplied example outputs but defeats the plain-3-coloring shortcut.
